My uncle, born in 1943, is the last remaining member of that generation in our family.

I recently sent him a family video—a collection of old photos set to music, capturing moments from my immediate family over the years. When I called him on a popular social networking service, he told me he had received the message and watched the video.

We talked about the health of our older relatives and the progress of his three grandchildren, who are now finishing school and entering the workforce. He also shared that he had undergone three surgeries to remove cancerous growths. It is remarkable that modern medicine has given him so many additional years.

I asked if he remembered a moment from long ago, when our family won a radio contest. Before television became widespread, radio was the center of daily life. My uncle had submitted the names of everyone in the family, and on the day of the announcement, we all gathered around the radio to listen.

The announcer said:

“인천시… 남구… 주안동… 246번지.”

Everyone grew excited.

Then he called my name.

My uncle threw me into the air in celebration. We traveled together to Seoul to claim the prize. But after deducting service fees and taxes, the reward had shrunk to the price of lunch for two.

I told my uncle this story again during our call. He didn’t remember it.

If something doesn’t touch your life directly, it fades from memory.

Growing up, I often heard my father tell the story of how his family escaped from North Korea.

His maternal uncle had walked most of the 100-plus miles from Seoul to 안변, 함경도 to find them and bring them south.

After arriving in South Korea, my father found work at a Japanese furniture company. When Japan surrendered at the end of World War II and its officials left, my father assumed responsibility for one of the manager’s homes.

He was only fifteen years and five months old at the time.

My uncle had a slightly different version of events.

He remembers his mother saying he was about one year old when the family left North Korea for Seoul. That would place their departure around 1944.

This raises questions: would that have given my father enough time to get established, earn the trust of local workers, and eventually occupy a house that once belonged to a company manager?

What we do know is that my father’s maternal uncle played a key role in guiding the family out of the North. We also know that my father worked for a Japanese furniture company, and that our family lived in that house well into the Korean War and even afterward.

What we don’t know is when exactly the maternal uncle arrived in North Korea to help them, or the precise moment the family left their home and resettled in Seoul.

I have no reason to believe my father or my uncle shared anything untrue. Rather, I believe both of their recollections are correct—pieces of a story that likely unfolded across several stages.

It is entirely possible that my father’s family traveled south in multiple groups: perhaps my grandfather and the older children left first to get established, followed by another group with younger siblings, and finally the youngest children and my grandmother.

This pattern would not be unusual. When we ourselves moved to Korea, my father went a month ahead to prepare things. And when we returned to Korea years later for an expatriate assignment, I left in January, with Sister K and the children following about two months later.

Instead of trying to force a single “official” version of the story—based on memories that naturally differ—I hope to capture our family history simply as it was told by those who lived it. Where dates or details are missing, I will record what is known and allow readers to imagine the rest.

My hope is that these memories serve as a reminder of how the God of Israel has guided our family—through war, through hardship, and into a new world filled with hope.
